name: Namdapha
image_query: Namdapha National Park Noa Dihing river
tagline: Lowland rainforest on the Noa-Dihing, beyond Miao
meta_description: Namdapha National Park guide: Deban and the Noa-Dihing, hoolock gibbons, hornbills, the Firmbase trek, Stilwell Road, permits, costs and how to reach Miao.
summary: Namdapha National Park in Changlang district protects about 1,985 sq km of forest rising from about 200 m to over 4,500 m on the Myanmar border. Base yourself at Miao or the forest rest house at Deban on the Noa-Dihing. Come November to March for birds, gibbons and dry trails; stay 3–4 nights.
intro: Namdapha is one of the largest protected areas in India and one of the least visited. Declared a national park and tiger reserve in 1983, it climbs from lowland evergreen rainforest along the Noa-Dihing river to temperate forest and snow on the Dapha Bum ridge. That range of altitude explains its reputation: tigers, leopards, clouded leopards and snow leopards have all been recorded inside one park.

For visitors, Namdapha means the lower forest. The town of Miao, on the Noa-Dihing at the park's western edge, has the field director's office, a small museum and simple hotels. From Miao a rough road runs about 25 km to Deban, where the forest rest house looks across the river into the park. From Deban, guided treks lead deeper to camps such as Haldibari and Firmbase.

This is not a safari park. There are no open jeep drives and big cats are almost never seen. What you get is real rainforest: hoolock gibbons calling at dawn, hornbills crossing the river, giant trees, leeches after rain and a silence broken only by birds. Come prepared to walk, accept simple rooms and food, and give it at least three nights.

highlights.title: Deban on the Noa-Dihing
highlights.text: The forest rest house at Deban stands above the river where the park begins. Mornings bring mist on the water, hornbills crossing and gibbons calling from the far bank. Most walks start with a river crossing here.

highlights.title: Hoolock gibbons at dawn
highlights.text: Namdapha is one of the best places in India to hear hoolock gibbons, India's only ape. Families call to each other across the canopy at first light, and patient walkers sometimes see them moving through the treetops.

highlights.title: Birds of the rainforest
highlights.text: Hornbills, babblers, laughingthrushes, broadbills and wren-babblers make Namdapha a serious birding site. A local bird guide helps enormously, since the forest is dense and many species are heard before they are seen.

highlights.title: Trek to Haldibari and Firmbase
highlights.text: Guided treks from Deban follow forest trails to camps at Haldibari and Firmbase, with river crossings, giant trees and nights in simple camps. They need permits, a guide and porters, and suit fit, prepared walkers.

highlights.title: Stilwell Road and Miao
highlights.text: The Second World War road from Ledo towards Burma passes through Jairampur and Nampong, south of Miao. A war cemetery near Jairampur and the Pangsau Pass on the border tell that history; access rules vary.

highlights.title: Miao's Tibetan settlement and museum
highlights.text: Miao has a Tibetan settlement known for carpets, and the park's small museum near the field director's office. Both fill a spare afternoon before or after Deban.

field_notes.fact: Namdapha is one of very few places in the world where four big cats have been recorded in the same park: the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard and snow leopard, thanks to its range from lowland forest to alpine ridges.
The Namdapha flying squirrel is known to science from a single specimen collected in the park in 1981. It has not been confirmed since and is listed as critically endangered.

The Ledo Road, later renamed the Stilwell Road, was built by Allied forces in the Second World War to link Ledo in Assam with the Burma Road to China. Its route crosses Arunachal through Jairampur and Nampong to the Pangsau Pass.

how_to_reach.text: Dibrugarh airport, with flights from Delhi, Kolkata and Guwahati, is the usual gateway. From there it is about 170 km and 5–6 hours to Miao through Tinsukia, Margherita and Jagun, then another hour on a rough road to Deban.

Shared Sumos and buses run from Tinsukia and Dibrugarh to Miao, mostly in the morning. Tinsukia and Margherita have the nearest useful rail connections. From Miao to Deban you need a hired jeep arranged locally or through the forest department.

The road crosses into Arunachal near Jagun, where permits are checked, then runs through Kharsang to Miao. The Miao–Deban road is unsealed and may be impassable after heavy rain. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Saver: the forest rest house at Deban, booked through the forest department in Miao, is the classic Namdapha stay: simple rooms with a river view, basic food and limited power. Miao has a few simple hotels and lodges at ₹1,500–3,000 a night. Comfort: a few community-run camps and lodges near Miao offer more comfortable rooms and guiding; ask us for the current options. Signature: there is no luxury lodge here; we focus on private naturalist guiding.
tips: Book the Deban rest house and your guide through the forest department in Miao well ahead.
Carry leech socks; after any rain you will need them, and salt helps remove leeches.
Bring binoculars and dull-coloured clothing; the forest rewards quiet, slow walkers.
Name Changlang district on your Inner Line Permit; foreigners need a Protected Area Permit.
Carry cash for the whole stay; there are no ATMs beyond Miao and few in Miao itself.

experiences.title: Dawn at Deban with hoolock gibbons
experiences.summary: Wake at Deban before sunrise, cross the Noa-Dihing with a forest guide and walk into the rainforest to hear and look for hoolock gibbons, hornbills and the dawn bird chorus.
body: Gibbons are loudest in the first hours after dawn. At Deban, families of hoolock gibbons call from the forest across the Noa-Dihing, a rising, whooping duet that carries for kilometres. With a forest guide you cross the river, by boat or on foot depending on the season, and walk quietly along trails into the forest, stopping to listen.

Seeing gibbons takes patience. They move high in the canopy and stop calling when disturbed. A good guide listens for them and positions you below their route. On the same walk you may see hornbills flying over the river, squirrels, and many birds of the lower canopy. Leeches are common, so wear leech socks and check yourself often.

Return to the rest house for breakfast by mid-morning. Wear dull colours, keep voices low and do not use flash or play calls. Park rules on routes and timings are set by the forest department and change, so follow your guide and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Will I see hoolock gibbons in Namdapha?
faqs.a: You will very likely hear them, and with patience and a good guide you may see them high in the canopy. Sightings are never guaranteed, and early morning is by far the best time.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to walk in Namdapha?
faqs.a: Yes. Walks inside the park are with forest staff or approved guides. Arrange them through the forest department in Miao or at Deban.
Yes, especially after rain and in the warmer months. Wear leech socks and long trousers, carry salt, and check yourself after every walk.

experiences.title: Rainforest trek to Haldibari and Firmbase
experiences.cost: Guide and porters ₹2,500–5,000 a day for a small group; park fees extra
experiences.summary: Walk from Deban into the heart of Namdapha with a forest guide and porters, camping at Haldibari and Firmbase among giant trees, river crossings and the sounds of the lowland rainforest.
body: The classic trek in Namdapha follows forest trails east from Deban into the park. Haldibari, a day's walk in, is a simple camp in the forest; Firmbase, further on, sits near the Noa-Dihing among tall trees. The route crosses streams and sometimes the river itself, climbs over ridges and passes through dense bamboo and evergreen forest.

This is a serious trip. You need permission from the forest department in Miao, a forest guide, porters to carry tents and food, and your own good boots and rain gear. Trails are muddy, leeches are everywhere after rain, and routes change when trees fall or river levels shift. Plan 3–5 days depending on how far you go and how much time you want for birds and wildlife.

The rewards are rare: nights in the forest, gibbons and hornbills overhead, and the chance of tracks of larger mammals. Carry all your rubbish out. Rules, fees and trail status change, so check current status before you travel and arrange the trek at least a few weeks ahead.

faqs.q: How hard is the Firmbase trek in Namdapha?
faqs.a: Moderate to hard. Altitudes are low, but trails are muddy, slippery and leech-infested, with river crossings and some steep sections. You need good fitness, boots with grip and rain gear.

faqs.q: How do I arrange a trek in Namdapha?
faqs.a: Contact the forest department in Miao for permission, then arrange a forest guide and porters through them or a local operator. Plan a few weeks ahead and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do you sleep on the Namdapha trek?
faqs.a: In simple camps such as Haldibari and Firmbase, usually in tents carried by porters or in basic forest shelters. Bring a warm sleeping bag; nights are cool in winter.

experiences.title: Stilwell Road, Jairampur and Pangsau
experiences.summary: Follow the Second World War road from Ledo towards Burma through Jairampur and Nampong, stopping at the war cemetery near Jairampur and, where allowed, the Pangsau Pass on the Myanmar border.
body: In 1942–45 Allied engineers and labourers built a road from Ledo in Assam over the hills into Burma, to reconnect India with the Burma Road to China. First called the Ledo Road and later the Stilwell Road after the American general who commanded the effort, it climbs through what is now Changlang district via Jairampur and Nampong to the Pangsau Pass on the border.

From Miao, a day's drive lets you trace part of this history. Near Jairampur, a Second World War cemetery holds graves of soldiers and workers who died building and defending the road. Further on, Nampong is the last town before the Pangsau Pass. A small lake near the pass is known locally as the Lake of No Return, linked by local accounts to wartime aircraft losses.

Access beyond Nampong and to the pass itself depends on permits and on the current rules for the border area; at times visitors have been allowed only on particular days or during the Pangsau Pass Winter Festival in January. Check current status before you travel, carry your permits and ID, and photograph only where allowed.

faqs.a: It is the Second World War road built from Ledo in Assam into Burma to connect India with the Burma Road to China. First called the Ledo Road, it was renamed after General Joseph Stilwell. Its route passes Jairampur and Nampong in Arunachal.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit the Pangsau Pass?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Access to the pass on the Myanmar border has depended on permits and current rules, and has been easiest during the Pangsau Pass Winter Festival in January. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Jairampur from Miao?
faqs.a: About 60–80 km, roughly 2–2.5 hours by road via Kharsang and Jagun. A full day covers Jairampur, Nampong and the return to Miao.

faqs.q: How do I reach Namdapha National Park?
faqs.a: Fly to Dibrugarh, then drive about 170 km and 5–6 hours via Tinsukia and Margherita to Miao. From Miao a rough road runs about 25 km to Deban, the main entry point. Shared Sumos and buses reach Miao; for Deban you need a hired jeep.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Namdapha?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian visitors need an Inner Line Permit listing Changlang district, and foreigners a Protected Area Permit. You also need park entry permission and fees from the forest department in Miao. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Namdapha?
faqs.a: November to March, when the forest is driest, trails are walkable and birding is good. April gets hot and wet. From May to September heavy rain and leeches make the park difficult, and access to Deban may close.

faqs.q: Can I see tigers in Namdapha?
faqs.a: Very unlikely. Tigers and other big cats have been recorded, but the forest is dense and there are no safari drives. Visitors come for birds, gibbons, the rainforest itself and the experience of walking in it.

faqs.q: Where do I stay in Namdapha?
faqs.a: Inside the park, the forest rest house at Deban is the main option, booked through the forest department in Miao. Miao has simple hotels and some community-run camps. Treks use simple camps at Haldibari and Firmbase.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Namdapha?
faqs.a: Three or four nights for Deban and day walks, or six to eight nights if you plan the trek to Firmbase. Add travel days from Dibrugarh at each end.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Namdapha?
faqs.a: Miao has some mobile coverage, but signal fades on the road to Deban and is absent inside the park. Tell family you will be offline and carry a printed copy of your permits and bookings.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Namdapha?
faqs.a: Leech socks, long trousers, boots with grip, a rain jacket, a headtorch, binoculars, a light warm layer for cool mornings, insect repellent and any medicines you need. Food is simple; carry snacks.

For older children who enjoy walking and do not mind leeches and basic rooms, yes. It is not suited to toddlers or anyone needing comfort and quick medical access, since the nearest good hospitals are in Assam.
